meta.case_name: New England Ski Resorts Association – Strategy

prompt.context: Our client is the association of New England ski resorts. It is 1985, and profitability of member resorts has been going down for two years. The association has hired us (1) to find out why and (2) to recommend what to do about it.
prompt.question: Why has profitability been declining at New England ski resorts, and what should the association do about it?

clarifying_info.q: Has the average price of lift tickets gone down?
Has the number of skiers gone down?
clarifying_info.a: Yes. It has plummeted over the last two years.

clarifying_info.q: Have fixed or variable costs gone up over the last two years?
Has the weather been a factor?
Are skiers going elsewhere, or is skiing becoming less popular overall?
clarifying_info.a: Skiing is as popular as ever, but more people are now going out west instead of skiing in New England.

clarifying_info.q: What caused the shift to western resorts?
clarifying_info.a: Airlines cut their fares, meaning people pay a smaller premium to fly out west.

framework: Start with the profitability equation: Revenue − Costs
Revenue = Price × Volume (skier-days); check each driver
Costs = Fixed + Variable; assess whether cost structure changed
Isolate which driver changed: price flat, costs flat → volume (skier count) is the problem
Diagnose why skier count fell: demand-side (skiing elsewhere, substitute activities, overall spending cuts) vs. supply-side (weather, capacity)
Identify root cause: lower airfares made western resorts relatively cheaper, pulling New England skiers westward
Develop solutions: restore skier volume, increase revenue per skier, or recover fixed costs via new revenue streams

questions.prompt: Where in the profitability equation is the problem?
questions.guidance: Candidate should decompose Profit = Revenue − Costs, then Revenue = Price × Volume. Price is flat, costs are flat, so the problem must be declining skier volume (number of skiers has plummeted). A strong candidate checks both sides quickly before drilling down.

questions.prompt: Why is the number of skiers declining? How would you diagnose this?
questions.guidance: Candidate should distinguish demand-side causes (people skiing elsewhere, substituting other recreation, cutting back overall) from supply-side causes (weather, snow quality). Good approach: compare ticket-sales trends at non-New-England resorts; if sales are up elsewhere, demand is shifting rather than falling overall. Interviewer confirms weather is fine, so demand shift is the right track.

questions.prompt: How would you find and survey people who used to ski in New England but no longer do?
questions.guidance: Rent mailing lists from ski magazines targeting subscribers in New England and New York. Conduct telephone or mail survey asking: frequency of skiing in New England, frequency skiing elsewhere, frequency of substitute activities (e.g., beach vacations), and whether habits changed in the last two years. Candidate should show practical research design thinking.

questions.prompt: If people are shifting to western resorts, what could cause that shift?
questions.guidance: Break down the cost of a ski vacation: equipment, transportation, lodging, lift tickets. Equipment, lodging, and lift tickets are roughly comparable between the Rockies and New England. Transportation is the key differentiator: New Englanders must fly west, which was historically expensive. Two explanations: (1) a strong economy makes people feel wealthier and willing to pay more; (2) airlines cut fares, reducing the price premium for going west. The interviewer confirms airlines cut fares.

questions.prompt: What would you recommend to restore profitability?
questions.guidance: Three levers: (1) Restore skier volume — reduce prices, offer regional season passes, improve the overall resort experience to compete with western destinations; (2) Increase revenue per skier — add lodging packages, equipment rentals/sales, lessons, dining; (3) Recover fixed costs via non-ski seasons — ski mountains are almost entirely fixed-cost operations (mountain, lifts, ski patrol, snowmaking) spread over only 3–4 winter months. Building summer amenities (golf courses, water slides, hiking, mountain biking) spreads fixed costs across more months and revenue streams.

brainstorming.prompt: What are other ways ski resorts could recover their largely fixed cost base beyond the ski season?

recommendation: Root cause is lower airline fares making western ski destinations relatively more affordable, drawing skiers away from New England resorts
Short term: introduce regional season passes and bundled resort packages (lodging + lift tickets) to improve value proposition versus western destinations
Medium term: develop year-round revenue streams (golf, summer recreation, events) to spread high fixed costs across all four seasons and reduce dependence on winter skier volume
risks: Capital investment in summer facilities may be substantial with uncertain demand
Discounted pricing or passes could erode revenue per skier if not carefully designed
Western resorts may continue to improve, maintaining their relative attractiveness even as airfares normalize
next_steps: Survey lapsed New England skiers to validate price-sensitivity and willingness to return under different pricing/package structures
Benchmark summer revenue programs at comparable mountain resorts to identify best-in-class models
Financial model the fixed-cost recovery impact of a 12-month operating calendar versus winter-only
